1	# Paper Framing — irt_equated_bench_regen
2	
3	## Target Venue
4	- Primary: ICLR 2027 (expected deadline ~October 2026)
5	
6	## Paper Type
7	Empirical analysis / psychometric characterization. Discovery paper, not methods paper. "DIF reveals benchmark structural problems," not "DIF detects contamination."
8	
9	## Core Claims (4 条, 可证伪)
10	
11	**Claim 1 (Temporal Comparability Concern)**: 38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations — they exhibit large DIF (ETS C, |Δ_MH|≥1.5) between 2023 and 2024-H1 model cohorts. This instability persists within every subject domain (within-subject C%=31-45%, avg 38.1%), is not a statistical artifact (random split sanity check: 0.18%), and correlates with domain-specific accuracy improvement (ρ=0.307, p=0.02). This means cross-temporal MMLU score comparisons carry uncontrolled item-level variance.
12	- Evidence: plan_001 (C%=31.3%, enrichment=0.96, sanity=0.18%), plan_014 (within-subject C%=38.1%)
13	- Honesty requirement: ρ=0.307 means "item instability" may mainly reflect "models got better at those domains" — we cannot decompose 38% into contamination vs capability improvement
14	
15	**Claim 2 (Ground Truth Meta-critique)**: Existing contamination detection literature validates against web-overlap/n-gram labels that measure global exposure (whether an item is publicly accessible), not differential contamination (whether an item functions differently across model cohorts). DIF enrichment≈1.0 against Li et al. labels is expected, not failure — these labels cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. This is a fundamental validation methodology gap: all work using web-overlap labels as ground truth for item-level detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind spot. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF can detect differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5, dose-response from p=0.3 to p=1.0).
16	- Evidence: plan_001 (enrichment=0.96), plan_011 (ΔTPR=+0.508, dose-response)
17	- Framing: aggressive — "the field's standard validation approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection"
18	
19	**Claim 3 (Semi-synthetic Validation Framework)**: The ΔTPR methodology — injecting known differential contamination into real response matrices and measuring detection power increase — provides a controlled validation infrastructure for any item-level contamination detector. Cross-subject matching (using total score on OTHER subjects as MH matching variable) eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 across all 5 tested subjects), while within-subject matching suffers from matching variable contamination (FPR inflation +0.186).
20	- Evidence: plan_011, plan_016 (ΔFPR=0.000 cross-subject, 4/5 subjects ΔTPR>0.3), plan_004 Step 2 (GSM8K ΔTPR=+0.818 standard, +0.517 external)
21	- Cross-benchmark: GSM8K replication confirms framework portability to single-domain math benchmarks
22	- Positioning: cross-subject matching is a practical methodological recommendation; cross-benchmark replication strengthens generalizability
23	
24	**Claim 4 (Downstream Impact — Four-Layer Finding)**: DIF as diagnostic lens, not quality filter. Four sub-findings:
25	1. **Benchmark redundancy**: ρ≈0.997 between full and stable-only rankings — MMLU rankings are extremely robust to 31% item removal, revealing massive measurement redundancy in the benchmark.
26	2. **DIF items = discriminative signal carriers**: DIF removal causes significantly MORE ranking disruption than random removal (z=-8 to -49σ, 21/21 conditions). DIF items carry 1.09× cross-cohort accuracy swing vs 0.96× for stable items — they concentrate the information that differentiates model generations.
27	3. **DIF as diagnostic lens**: DIF identifies which items' functioning changes most across model generations → reveals which capability dimensions drive ranking shifts. Not "find bad items and remove" but "understand what changed and why." Model-specific patterns: phi-3/llama-3 gain +700-850 ranks from DIF items, mistral merges lose -400 to -587.
28	4. **Cross-benchmark validation — DIF captures capability, not contamination**: On GSM8K (1,319 items × 6,702 models), DIF flags anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gap (r=−0.478, p=0.005; partial r=−0.385 controlling accuracy; permutation p=0.014). Contaminated models (high GSM8K-GSM1K gap: Phi, Gemma families) perform WORSE on DIF items. DIF captures genuine capability-discriminative items that contamination cannot fake — contamination produces shallow performance gains concentrated on non-DIF items. N=33 matched models, leave-one-out robust (min |r|=0.374).
29	- Evidence: plan_017 (z=-8 to -49σ, ρ=0.996-0.999), plan_004 Step 3 (r=−0.478, p=0.005, 33 models)
30	- Growing Pains互补: "Growing Pains uses anchor items for efficient evaluation; our DIF diagnostic tells them which anchor items are degrading" — mutual value positioning
31	- Caveats (→ limitations): super-family analysis limited to N≥20 families; GSM1K validation N=33 (CI wide); contamination gap is proxy, not ground truth
32	
33	## Story Spine
34	
35	**Problem**: LLM benchmarks implicitly assume temporal score comparability — when we say "Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU," we presume both scores reflect the same latent construct. But do they? Item-level behavioral drift across model generations could silently erode this assumption.
36	
37	**Approach**: We apply Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis — a classical psychometric tool for detecting item-level behavioral anomalies — to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items), the largest-scale DIF analysis on LLM benchmarks to date.
38	
39	**What we find**: Three discoveries, each a contribution:
40	
41	1. **38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable** across model generations (ETS C DIF, temporal cohorts). This persists within every subject domain (31-45% per subject), is not statistical noise (random split: 0.18%), and cannot be eliminated by three structural corrections (matched-ability, IRT θ-conditioning, bifactor pre-check). The instability correlates with capability improvement (ρ=0.307) — models got better at those domains, changing how items function.
42	
43	2. **The field's standard validation approach has a blind spot**: Web-overlap contamination labels (Li et al.) measure whether an item is publicly accessible — a global, model-agnostic property. DIF detects whether an item functions differently across model cohorts — a dynamic, group-specific signal. Enrichment≈1.0 between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is expected when most items have equal global exposure (MMLU on Common Crawl since 2020). Semi-synthetic injection proves DIF works (ΔTPR=+0.508) — the problem is the ground truth, not the detector. Any contamination detection paper validating against web-overlap labels at the item level has the same issue.
44	
45	3. **A semi-synthetic validation framework** that injects controlled differential contamination into real response matrices, measuring ΔTPR as the detection power metric. Cross-subject matching eliminates the matching variable contamination problem (ΔFPR=0.000). This infrastructure is reusable for validating any item-level contamination detector.
46	
47	4. **DIF is a diagnostic lens, not a quality filter**. MMLU rankings are massively redundant (ρ≈0.997 after 31% removal), but DIF items concentrate the discriminative signal that differentiates model generations (removal disrupts rankings MORE than random, z=-8 to -49σ). Cross-benchmark validation on GSM8K confirms: DIF flags anti-correlate with contamination (r=−0.478, p=0.005) — contaminated models can't fake performance on DIF items, which capture genuine capability differences. DIF identifies which capability dimensions are changing — complementing Growing Pains' anchor-item approach by detecting which anchors are degrading.
48	
49	**Headline result**: "Psychometric analysis of METABENCH reveals that 38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations. Web-overlap contamination labels do not capture this differential signal (enrichment≈1.0), while semi-synthetic injection confirms detection capability (ΔTPR=+0.508 on MMLU, +0.818 on GSM8K). Cross-benchmark validation using GSM1K contamination gaps shows DIF flags anti-correlate with contamination (r=−0.478, p=0.005): DIF captures genuine capability-discriminative items that contamination cannot replicate. We provide a reusable validation framework with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000)."
50	
51	## Empirical Observation: Structural Constraints on DIF in LLM Benchmarks
52	
53	Systematic experimentation reveals that three structural improvements — matched-ability cohort design (plan_001b), IRT θ-conditioning (plan_012, r=0.9986), and bifactor pre-check (plan_014, within-subject C%=38.1%) — all fail to reduce temporal DIF baseline FPR below 31% while maintaining detection power. This is an empirical observation, not a formal impossibility result. The constraints arise from: (a) unidimensional IRT limitations in modeling 57-subject multidimensional ability, (b) statistical power requirements (N≥80, δ≥1.4), and (c) inability to separate ability confounding from genuine item-level changes. Higher-level methods (MIMIC, propensity-score matching, multidimensional IRT) may address individual constraints — future work.
54	
55	## Venue Fit
56	
57	- **ICLR 2027**: Good fit — empirical analysis of evaluation methodology, psychometric rigor, large-scale characterization. Risk: ML reviewers may not be familiar with DIF/IRT. Mitigation: §3 provides self-contained DIF primer with ML translations.

Our contributions are: (1) the empirical finding of 38% instability, (2) the ground truth meta-critique affecting the field, (3) the semi-synthetic framework. # Paper Framing — irt_equated_bench_regen

## Target Venue
- Primary: ICLR 2027 (expected deadline ~October 2026)

## Paper Type
Empirical analysis / psychometric characterization. Discovery paper, not methods paper. "DIF reveals benchmark structural problems," not "DIF detects contamination."

## Core Claims (4 条, 可证伪)

**Claim 1 (Temporal Comparability Concern)**: 38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations — they exhibit large DIF (ETS C, |Δ_MH|≥1.5) between 2023 and 2024-H1 model cohorts. This instability persists within every subject domain (within-subject C%=31-45%, avg 38.1%), is not a statistical artifact (random split sanity check: 0.18%), and correlates with domain-specific accuracy improvement (ρ=0.307, p=0.02). This means cross-temporal MMLU score comparisons carry uncontrolled item-level variance.
- Evidence: plan_001 (C%=31.3%, enrichment=0.96, sanity=0.18%), plan_014 (within-subject C%=38.1%)
- Honesty requirement: ρ=0.307 means "item instability" may mainly reflect "models got better at those domains" — we cannot decompose 38% into contamination vs capability improvement

**Claim 2 (Ground Truth Meta-critique)**: Existing contamination detection literature validates against web-overlap/n-gram labels that measure global exposure (whether an item is publicly accessible), not differential contamination (whether an item functions differently across model cohorts). DIF enrichment≈1.0 against Li et al. labels is expected, not failure — these labels cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. This is a fundamental validation methodology gap: all work using web-overlap labels as ground truth for item-level detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind spot. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF can detect differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5, dose-response from p=0.3 to p=1.0).
- Evidence: plan_001 (enrichment=0.96), plan_011 (ΔTPR=+0.508, dose-response)
- Framing: aggressive — "the field's standard validation approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection"

**Claim 3 (Semi-synthetic Validation Framework)**: The ΔTPR methodology — injecting known differential contamination into real response matrices and measuring detection power increase — provides a controlled validation infrastructure for any item-level contamination detector. Cross-subject matching (using total score on OTHER subjects as MH matching variable) eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 across all 5 tested subjects), while within-subject matching suffers from matching variable contamination (FPR inflation +0.186).
- Evidence: plan_011, plan_016 (ΔFPR=0.000 cross-subject, 4/5 subjects ΔTPR>0.3), plan_004 Step 2 (GSM8K ΔTPR=+0.818 standard, +0.517 external)
- Cross-benchmark: GSM8K replication confirms framework portability to single-domain math benchmarks
- Positioning: cross-subject matching is a practical methodological recommendation; cross-benchmark replication strengthens generalizability

**Claim 4 (Downstream Impact — Four-Layer Finding)**: DIF as diagnostic lens, not quality filter. Four sub-findings:
1. **Benchmark redundancy**: ρ≈0.997 between full and stable-only rankings — MMLU rankings are extremely robust to 31% item removal, revealing massive measurement redundancy in the benchmark.
2. **DIF items = discriminative signal carriers**: DIF removal causes significantly MORE ranking disruption than random removal (z=-8 to -49σ, 21/21 conditions). DIF items carry 1.09× cross-cohort accuracy swing vs 0.96× for stable items — they concentrate the information that differentiates model generations.
3. **DIF as diagnostic lens**: DIF identifies which items' functioning changes most across model generations → reveals which capability dimensions drive ranking shifts. Not "find bad items and remove" but "understand what changed and why." Model-specific patterns: phi-3/llama-3 gain +700-850 ranks from DIF items, mistral merges lose -400 to -587.
4. **Cross-benchmark validation — DIF captures capability, not contamination**: On GSM8K (1,319 items × 6,702 models), DIF flags anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gap (r=−0.478, p=0.005; partial r=−0.385 controlling accuracy; permutation p=0.014). Contaminated models (high GSM8K-GSM1K gap: Phi, Gemma families) perform WORSE on DIF items. DIF captures genuine capability-discriminative items that contamination cannot fake — contamination produces shallow performance gains concentrated on non-DIF items. N=33 matched models, leave-one-out robust (min |r|=0.374).
- Evidence: plan_017 (z=-8 to -49σ, ρ=0.996-0.999), plan_004 Step 3 (r=−0.478, p=0.005, 33 models)
- Growing Pains互补: "Growing Pains uses anchor items for efficient evaluation; our DIF diagnostic tells them which anchor items are degrading" — mutual value positioning
- Caveats (→ limitations): super-family analysis limited to N≥20 families; GSM1K validation N=33 (CI wide); contamination gap is proxy, not ground truth

## Story Spine

**Problem**: LLM benchmarks implicitly assume temporal score comparability — when we say "Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU," we presume both scores reflect the same latent construct. But do they? Item-level behavioral drift across model generations could silently erode this assumption.

**Approach**: We apply Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis — a classical psychometric tool for detecting item-level behavioral anomalies — to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items), the largest-scale DIF analysis on LLM benchmarks to date.

**What we find**: Three discoveries, each a contribution:

1. **38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable** across model generations (ETS C DIF, temporal cohorts). This persists within every subject domain (31-45% per subject), is not statistical noise (random split: 0.18%), and cannot be eliminated by three structural corrections (matched-ability, IRT θ-conditioning, bifactor pre-check). The instability correlates with capability improvement (ρ=0.307) — models got better at those domains, changing how items function.

2. **The field's standard validation approach has a blind spot**: Web-overlap contamination labels (Li et al.) measure whether an item is publicly accessible — a global, model-agnostic property. DIF detects whether an item functions differently across model cohorts — a dynamic, group-specific signal. Enrichment≈1.0 between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is expected when most items have equal global exposure (MMLU on Common Crawl since 2020). Semi-synthetic injection proves DIF works (ΔTPR=+0.508) — the problem is the ground truth, not the detector. Any contamination detection paper validating against web-overlap labels at the item level has the same issue.

3. **A semi-synthetic validation framework** that injects controlled differential contamination into real response matrices, measuring ΔTPR as the detection power metric. Cross-subject matching eliminates the matching variable contamination problem (ΔFPR=0.000). This infrastructure is reusable for validating any item-level contamination detector.

4. **DIF is a diagnostic lens, not a quality filter**. MMLU rankings are massively redundant (ρ≈0.997 after 31% removal), but DIF items concentrate the discriminative signal that differentiates model generations (removal disrupts rankings MORE than random, z=-8 to -49σ). Cross-benchmark validation on GSM8K confirms: DIF flags anti-correlate with contamination (r=−0.478, p=0.005) — contaminated models can't fake performance on DIF items, which capture genuine capability differences. DIF identifies which capability dimensions are changing — complementing Growing Pains' anchor-item approach by detecting which anchors are degrading.

**Headline result**: "Psychometric analysis of METABENCH reveals that 38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations. Web-overlap contamination labels do not capture this differential signal (enrichment≈1.0), while semi-synthetic injection confirms detection capability (ΔTPR=+0.508 on MMLU, +0.818 on GSM8K). Cross-benchmark validation using GSM1K contamination gaps shows DIF flags anti-correlate with contamination (r=−0.478, p=0.005): DIF captures genuine capability-discriminative items that contamination cannot replicate. We provide a reusable validation framework with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000)."

## Empirical Observation: Structural Constraints on DIF in LLM Benchmarks

Systematic experimentation reveals that three structural improvements — matched-ability cohort design (plan_001b), IRT θ-conditioning (plan_012, r=0.9986), and bifactor pre-check (plan_014, within-subject C%=38.1%) — all fail to reduce temporal DIF baseline FPR below 31% while maintaining detection power. This is an empirical observation, not a formal impossibility result. The constraints arise from: (a) unidimensional IRT limitations in modeling 57-subject multidimensional ability, (b) statistical power requirements (N≥80, δ≥1.4), and (c) inability to separate ability confounding from genuine item-level changes. Higher-level methods (MIMIC, propensity-score matching, multidimensional IRT) may address individual constraints — future work.

## Venue Fit

- **ICLR 2027**: Good fit — empirical analysis of evaluation methodology, psychometric rigor, large-scale characterization. Risk: ML reviewers may not be familiar with DIF/IRT. Mitigation: §3 provides self-contained DIF primer with ML translations.
- **Novelty concern**: DIF itself is not new (1988). Our contributions are: (1) the empirical finding of 38% instability, (2) the ground truth meta-critique affecting the field, (3) the semi-synthetic framework. Frame as "bringing mature psychometric tools to characterize an urgent ML evaluation problem."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns (updated for pivot)

1. **"38% could just mean models got better"** — Yes, partially. ρ=0.307 confirms correlation. We discuss this honestly. The contribution is the finding itself: benchmarks have massive item-level behavioral drift, regardless of cause.

2. **"Ground truth critique is obvious — of course web labels don't capture differential effects"** — Not obvious: the field routinely uses these labels for item-level validation. We provide the first empirical demonstration with both the enrichment≈1.0 result and the semi-synthetic proof of concept.

3. **"Semi-synthetic injection is artificial"** — We inject into real response matrices (not simulated), preserving real ability distributions and item characteristics. The mechanism (incorrect→correct flipping) is a simplification acknowledged in limitations.

4. **"DIF power is only sufficient for large effects"** — Large effects are precisely what threaten benchmark validity most. Operational region: N≥80, δ≥1.4, TPR=0.68-0.80.

5. **"Only validated on MMLU"** — Partially addressed: GSM8K replication (METABENCH 1,319 items × 6,702 models) confirms semi-synthetic framework portability (ΔTPR=+0.818) and temporal DIF pattern (C%=18.9%). GSM1K contamination gap validation (N=33) provides cross-benchmark evidence. Full generalization to diverse benchmarks remains future work.

6. **"Higher methods (MIMIC, propensity-score) could solve the confounding"** — Acknowledged as future work. We frame our three-attempt negative results as "empirical observation" that motivates these directions, not as impossibility.

## Dropped from Original Framing

- **Ensemble (Claim 2 old)**: plan_003a/b/c never executed. Future work.
- **Regeneration (Claim 3 old)**: Bifactor killed by plan_014 pre-check. Dropped entirely.
- **RL robustness**: Theoretically motivated but N=13 insufficient. Limitations disclosure, not claim.
- **Detection as primary contribution**: Pivoted from "we detect contamination" to "we characterize benchmark properties."

This is a detailed strategic evaluation request from the Director. Let me carefully analyze both issues.

## 议题 1: D014 负相关 claim 强度评估

### 1. Claim 说服力分析

r = −0.478, N = 33, p = 0.005

95% CI for r = −0.478 at N = 33:
Using Fisher z-transformation:
z = arctanh(r) = arctanh(-0.478) ≈ -0.519
SE(z) = 1/sqrt(N-3) = 1/sqrt(30) ≈ 0.183


95% CI for z: [-0.877, -0.161]
Convert back to r: [-0.705, -0.160]

So the 95% confidence interval spans from about -0.70 to -0.16, which is quite wide — the lower bound suggests a strong negative effect while the upper bound indicates something much weaker. The interval doesn't cross zero, which supports statistical significance, but the breadth reveals considerable uncertainty about the true effect size.

For the paper, I should frame r = -0.478 with CI [-0.70, -0.16] as statistically significant but with a wide range that could represent anything from weak to strong effects — "suggestive but not conclusive" captures this appropriately.

Now I'm questioning whether the "contamination can't fake" claim holds up. The DIF advantage metric compares performance on DIF-C items versus non-DIF items, and nearly all models show negative values, meaning DIF-C items are systematically harder. There's also a positive correlation between contamination gap and overall GSM8K accuracy — models with larger contamination gaps tend to score higher on GSM8K. But wait, that's backwards from what I'd expect if contamination were just inflating scores. Let me reconsider what's actually happening with the METAB results.

The DIF advantage comes from METABENCH response data while the contamination gap is measured from the GSM1K paper — they're independent measurements. Even controlling for GSM8K accuracy from the paper, the partial correlation stays significant at r = -0.385. But I'm controlling for the wrong accuracy metric here. The real issue might be item difficulty: if DIF-C items are harder and contaminated models concentrate their advantage on easier items, I'd see a negative correlation regardless of whether contamination is actually causing the effect.

To test this properly, I'd need to match each DIF-C item with non-DIF items of similar difficulty and recompute the advantage. There's also a model family confound — Phi and Gemma families show both high contamination gaps and specific weaknesses on certain question types, so the correlation could reflect family-level characteristics rather than contamination itself. The report doesn't show a single family driving the trend and the partial correlation holds up, but with only 33 models I don't have much statistical power to control for family effects. There's also an accuracy range issue where models with higher contamination gaps cluster in a particular performance band.

The real question is whether the negative correlation stems from contamination specifically or from a broader pattern where shallow, memorized knowledge fails on harder items — which would happen regardless of the source of that shallowness. Given the small sample size and wide confidence interval, I need to be careful about how I position this finding.

I think this works best as a supporting detail within the DIF-as-diagnostic argument rather than standing alone as its own claim. It provides useful cross-benchmark evidence without overreaching beyond what the data can support.

Looking at how this connects to the other findings: DIF items are highly discriminative across models, contaminated models underperform specifically on these items, and together these suggest contamination prevents models from accessing the deeper knowledge that DIF items require.

Now I'm working through how to handle the negative results systematically. The web-overlap enrichment finding directly supports the ground truth critique in Claim 2, so that belongs in the main results section.

The matched-ability ablation confirms the enrichment pattern holds across ability ranges, which strengthens the core finding but is less essential—a sentence in the main text with the full details in the appendix would work. The IRT conditioning check...

Actually, let me reconsider plan_014. The within-subject DIF result showing C% = 38.1% is genuinely important for Claim 1 because it demonstrates that item-level instability persists even when controlling for subject effects, ruling out a simple cross-subject confound. The bifactor direction failure is a separate negative finding, but the core result itself supports the temporal instability narrative and belongs in the main text.

For plan_017, the DIF removal experiment revealing that removing these items causes MORE ranking disruption than random removal is another case where the original hypothesis failed but the finding strongly supports the pivot—it shows DIF items carry meaningful signal rather than being noise to filter out. The extreme z-scores here are a key contribution.

Now looking at plan_004 Step 3 with the negative correlation...

this also inverts the expected direction but fits the cross-benchmark validation narrative where DIF acts as a capability discriminator. I'm organizing these into the main text with supporting figures.

So the pattern is clear: the story-supporting negatives—enrichment near 1.0, within-subject C% at 38.1%, DIF removal disruption, and the cross-benchmark correlation—all belong prominently in the main narrative because they validate the pivot claims, even though they contradicted the original hypotheses.

The real concern I need to address is the risk that reviewers see this as post-hoc rationalization rather than genuine discovery. I should make the chronological sequence explicit, ground the pivot in the data itself rather than narrative convenience, and show that each reframing emerged from what the results actually revealed.

import numpy as np

r = -0.478
n = 33
z = np.arctanh(r)
se = 1 / np.sqrt(n - 3)
ci_z_lo = z - 1.96 * se
ci_z_hi = z + 1.96 * se
ci_r_lo = np.tanh(ci_z_lo)
ci_r_hi = np.tanh(ci_z_hi)
print(f'r = {r}, N = {n}')

print(f'CI width: {ci_r_hi - ci_r_lo:.3f}')

# Effect size interpretation
print(f'\nCohen guidelines: small=0.1, medium=0.3, large=0.5')
print(f'|r|={abs(r):.3f} is between medium and large')
print(f'But CI upper bound |r|={abs(ci_r_hi):.3f} is only small-to-medium')

# Power analysis: what N needed for r=-0.478 to have CI not crossing -0.3?
for n_test in [40, 50, 60, 80, 100]:
    se_t = 1 / np.sqrt(n_test - 3)

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Load data
df = pd.read_csv('gsm1k_dif_correlation.csv')
print('=== Item difficulty confound check ===')
print(f'Models: {len(df)}')
print(f'Mean DIF advantage: {df[\"dif_advantage\"].mean():.4f}')
print(f'Std DIF advantage: {df[\"dif_advantage\"].std():.4f}')

# Check if gap correlates with overall METABENCH accuracy
# (not the GSM1K-paper accuracy)
metabench_acc = (df['acc_dif_c'] * 249 + df['acc_non_dif'] * 1070) / 1319
r_gap_mb, p_gap_mb = stats.pearsonr(df['gap'], metabench_acc)
print(f'\nGap vs METABENCH overall accuracy: r={r_gap_mb:.4f}, p={p_gap_mb:.4f}')

r_gap_paper, p_gap_paper = stats.pearsonr(df['gap'], df['gsm8k_acc'])
print(f'Gap vs Paper GSM8K accuracy: r={r_gap_paper:.4f}, p={p_gap_paper:.4f}')

# Check: is DIF advantage correlated with overall accuracy?
r_acc_da, p_acc_da = stats.pearsonr(metabench_acc, df['dif_advantage'])
print(f'METABENCH acc vs DIF advantage: r={r_acc_da:.4f}, p={p_acc_da:.4f}')

# Multiple regression: DIF advantage ~ gap + metabench_acc
from numpy.linalg import lstsq
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(df)), df['gap'].values, metabench_acc.values])
y = df['dif_advantage'].values
beta, _, _, _ = lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
print(f'\nMultiple regression: DIF_adv = {beta[0]:.4f} + {beta[1]:.4f}*gap + {beta[2]:.4f}*mb_acc')

# Partial correlation: gap vs DIF_adv controlling METABENCH acc (not paper acc)
slope_da, int_da, _, _, _ = stats.linregress(metabench_acc, y)
resid_da = y - (slope_da * metabench_acc + int_da)
slope_gap, int_gap, _, _, _ = stats.linregress(metabench_acc, df['gap'].values)
resid_gap = df['gap'].values - (slope_gap * metabench_acc + int_gap)
r_partial_mb, p_partial_mb = stats.pearsonr(resid_gap, resid_da)
print(f'Partial r (controlling METABENCH acc): r={r_partial_mb:.4f}, p={p_partial_mb:.4f}')

# Check: contaminated models accuracy distribution
print(f'\nTop 5 gap models:')
for _, row in df.head(5).iterrows():
    mb_acc = (row['acc_dif_c'] * 249 + row['acc_non_dif'] * 1070) / 1319
    print(f'  {row[\"model_name_gsm1k\"]}: gap={row[\"gap\"]:.3f}, paper_acc={row[\"gsm8k_acc\"]:.3f}, mb_acc={mb_acc:.3f}')
print(f'Bottom 3 gap models:')
for _, row in df.tail(3).iterrows():
    mb_acc = (row['acc_dif_c'] * 249 + row['acc_non_dif'] * 1070) / 1319
    print(f'  {row[\"model_name_gsm1k\"]}: gap={row[\"gap\"]:.3f}, paper_acc={row[\"gsm8k_acc\"]:.3f}, mb_acc={mb_acc:.3f}')
"

Very informative results. Let me analyze:

1. **METABENCH acc vs DIF advantage: r = -0.637, p = 0.0001** — This is critical! DIF advantage is STRONGLY negatively correlated with overall accuracy. Higher-accuracy models show MORE negative DIF advantage (DIF-C items are proportionally harder for them). This is a classic item difficulty × ability interaction effect.

2. **Gap vs METABENCH overall accuracy: r = 0.295, p = 0.095** — Gap is weakly positively correlated with METABENCH accuracy (not significant at 0.05). 

3. **Partial r (controlling METABENCH acc): r = -0.394, p = 0.023** — Even after accounting for overall accuracy, the gap-DIF advantage relationship persists and remains significant. This tells me the gap effect isn't just a byproduct of accuracy differences.

4. **Multiple regression**: DIF_adv = -0.038 - 0.674*gap - 0.128*mb_acc. The gap coefficient is substantially larger than the accuracy coefficient, indicating that gap is a stronger independent predictor of DIF advantage than overall performance level.

Now I'm considering whether item difficulty itself could be the underlying confound. The causal story might flow through accuracy — harder DIF-C items reveal negative advantages even in high-accuracy models, and since gap correlates weakly with accuracy, this could indirectly produce the negative gap-DIF correlation. But the partial correlation already rules out that full mediation pathway. There's a deeper mechanism at play, possibly related to how gap itself might reflect inflated accuracy — models whose GSM8K performance exceeds their true reasoning ability might systematically struggle on harder items because their advantage stems from memorization rather than genuine understanding.

The permutation test is the key evidence here: DIF-C items specifically produce a stronger correlation than random hard item subsets would, suggesting the designation itself matters beyond just difficulty. This points to something particular about how contaminated models fail on these items.

For my response, I need to be precise about claim strength — the correlation is suggestive rather than conclusive, with a confidence interval that includes small effects. The "contamination can't fake" argument has some merit given the partial correlation and permutation results, but I should acknowledge the item difficulty confound is real and the evidence is more nuanced than the original claim suggests.

On the second issue, I'm categorizing the negative results by their narrative role — some directly support the story while others need careful positioning to avoid overstating weak findings.

The plan_001 enrichment result anchors Claim 2, plan_014's within-subject instability supports Claim 1, and plan_017's downstream impact grounds Claim 4. Plan_001b's replicability and plan_004's inverted direction both strengthen the narrative, though the latter needs careful framing as a fourth layer. Plan_012 is purely ablative and belongs in the appendix. The real risk here is that a reviewer might see this as post-hoc storytelling — taking failures and reframing them as discoveries — so I need to be transparent about which results were predicted versus exploratory.

## 深度审查：D014 Claim 强度 + 阴性结果处理策略

---

## 议题 1：r = −0.478 Claim 强度评估

### 1.1 CI 宽度与说服力

95% CI (Fisher z 变换): **[−0.71, −0.16]**，宽度 0.54。

- 点估计 |r| = 0.478 处于 Cohen medium-to-large 之间
- **但 CI 上界 |r| = 0.16 仅为 small effect**——审稿人可以合理质疑"真实效应可能很小"
- 要使 CI 下界不跨 -0.30，需 N ≈ 100（当前 N=33 远远不够）
- **结论：suggestive，不是 conclusive。** 论文中必须报告 CI，不能仅报 p=0.005

### 1.2 "Contamination can't fake" 是否 overclaiming？

**是的，存在 item difficulty confound，但 partial correlation 部分化解。**

独立验证发现：
- **DIF advantage 与 METABENCH overall accuracy 强负相关：r = −0.637, p = 0.0001**——DIF-C items 对所有模型都更难，高准确率模型的 DIF disadvantage 反而更大
- **Gap 与 METABENCH accuracy 弱正相关：r = 0.295, p = 0.095**——contamination gap 大的模型 accuracy 略高
- **因果链风险：gap → (弱) 高 accuracy → (强) 更负 DIF advantage**。这不需要 contamination-specific 机制，只需要"hard items discriminate more against inflated accuracy"

**但：**
- Partial r 控制 METABENCH accuracy 后仍显著：**r = −0.394, p = 0.023**——gap 的贡献超出 accuracy 能解释的范围
- Permutation test p = 0.014——DIF-C 的特异性超过随机 249 items，不仅是"任意难题子集"
- Multiple regression: DIF_adv = −0.038 − 0.674×gap − 0.128×mb_acc，gap 系数绝对值 > accuracy 系数

**建议措辞**：从 "contamination can't fake" 降级为 **"DIF-C items resist contamination-based performance gains (r = −0.478, 95% CI [−0.71, −0.16]; partial r = −0.394 controlling overall accuracy)"**。加 caveat："item difficulty confound cannot be fully excluded at N=33; replication with larger matched sample needed."

### 1.3 叙事定位

**维持 Claim 4 第四层子发现，不升级为独立 Claim 5。**

理由：
- CI 太宽，不足以承载独立 claim 的证据标准
- Item difficulty confound 未完全排除
- 作为 Claim 4 四层论证的一层，与 plan_017（z = −8 to −49σ）形成 convergent evidence，说服力远强于单独使用
- 如果独立为 Claim 5，审稿人单独攻击 N=33 就能削弱整个 claim；嵌入四层结构中则不会

### 1.4 与 plan_017 的协同论证

**两者组合的逻辑链：**
1. plan_017: DIF items 是 discriminative signal carriers（移除比随机更 disruptive）→ DIF items 有结构性作用
2. Step 3: 高 contamination-gap 模型在 DIF items 上相对更弱 → contamination 不能复制 DIF items 所测量的能力
3. 组合结论：DIF 标记的 items 捕捉的是 genuine capability differences，contamination 产生的表面提升集中在 non-DIF items 上

**协同力度评估：plan_017 (strong, z = −8 to −49σ, 全部 5,227 models) + Step 3 (suggestive, r = −0.478, N=33) = moderately compelling。** plan_017 是坚实基础，Step 3 添加 contamination 维度但不是承重墙。如果 Step 3 被审稿人攻破，plan_017 的结论独立成立。这是正确的架构——不要让弱证据承重。

---

## 议题 2：6 个阴性结果论文处理策略

### 系统分类

| 实验 | 角色 | 位置 | 服务的 Claim | 处理方式 |
|------|------|------|-------------|---------|
| plan_001 enrichment=0.96 | **Story foundation** | Main text §4 | Claim 2 | 占 1-2 段，是 ground truth meta-critique 的实证基石。"We find enrichment ≈ 1.0, demonstrating that web-overlap labels do not capture differential item functioning." |
| plan_001b quintile enrichment≈1.0 | **Ablation** | Main text 1句 + Appendix table | Claim 2 | "This holds across all ability quintiles (Appendix A.x)." 一句话在 main text，详细数据在 appendix |
| plan_012 θ-conditioning r=0.9986 | **Ablation** | Appendix only | §Structural constraints | "IRT θ-conditioning yields r=0.9986 with total score, offering no improvement." 纯 appendix，不进 main text |
| plan_014 within-subject C%=38.1% | **Story supporting** | Main text §4 | Claim 1 | 这实际是 **positive for pivot narrative**——证明 DIF 在 subject 内部依然存在。"Within-subject analysis confirms item-level instability persists within every domain (range 31-45%, mean 38.1%)." |
| plan_017 DIF removal > random | **Story supporting** | Main text §5 | Claim 4 | 同样是 **positive for pivot narrative**——"negative but informative" = DIF items 是信号载体。至少占 1 段 + fig_4 |
| plan_004 Step 3 r=−0.478 | **Story supporting (inverted)** | Main text §5 | Claim 4 layer 4 | 方向反转但 informative。1 段 + scatter plot。诚实报告假设和实际方向的差异 |

### 无 claim-weakening negative

当前 6 个阴性结果中**没有一个直接削弱现有 claims**。原因是 D011 pivot 已经将叙事从"DIF detects contamination"转向"DIF characterizes benchmark properties"——所有原来的"检测失败"都成了新叙事的支撑证据。

### ⚠️ 关键风险："post-hoc storytelling" 攻击面

审稿人最可能的攻击不是任何单个 negative，而是**整体模式**："你尝试了 5 种检测方法都失败了，然后把失败重新包装为'发现'。这是 rationalization，不是 discovery。"

**预防策略：**
1. **不要隐藏 chronological sequence**——在论文中明确写："We initially hypothesized that DIF could detect contaminated items. Three structural improvements (matched-ability, IRT θ-conditioning, bifactor) failed to reduce baseline DIF below 31%. This led us to investigate what the persistent DIF actually captures."
2. **让数据驱动 pivot，不是 narrative desire**——pivot 的触发点是 plan_011 的 semi-synthetic success (ΔTPR=+0.508)，不是"我们想换个说法"。plan_011 证明 DIF 作为方法是有效的，只是 ground truth labels 不对。
3. **明确区分 "we changed our question" vs "we rationalized failure"**：原来的 question 是 "can DIF detect contamination?" → 负面。新 question 是 "what does DIF reveal about benchmark properties?" → 正面。Key difference: 新 question 有独立的新证据（plan_017 z=-49σ, plan_004 Step 3 r=-0.478），不是对旧数据的重新解读。

### Main text vs Appendix 优先级排序

**Main text（按论文章节顺序）：**
1. plan_001 enrichment=0.96 — §4 Results, Claim 2 核心
2. plan_014 within-subject C%=38.1% — §4 Results, Claim 1 强化
3. plan_017 DIF removal z=-49σ — §5 Downstream, Claim 4 核心
4. plan_004 Step 3 r=-0.478 — §5 Cross-benchmark, Claim 4 layer 4
5. plan_001b quintile (1 句 reference to appendix)

**Appendix：**
6. plan_001b 详细数据 — Appendix A.x
7. plan_012 θ-conditioning — Appendix A.y（"Structural Constraints" section）

### 一句话总结

5/6 阴性结果在 pivot 后变为 story-supporting evidence，1/6 纯 ablation 放 appendix。无 claim-weakening negative。主要风险是"post-hoc storytelling"攻击面——需要在论文中诚实呈现 chronological discovery process 来预防。

# Paper Framing — irt_equated_bench_regen

## Target Venue
- Primary: ICLR 2027 (expected deadline ~October 2026)

## Paper Type
Empirical analysis / psychometric characterization. Discovery paper, not methods paper. "DIF reveals benchmark structural problems," not "DIF detects contamination."

## Core Claims (4 条, 可证伪)

**Claim 1 (Temporal Comparability Concern)**: 28–38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations — they exhibit large DIF (ETS C, |Δ_MH|≥1.5) between 2023 and 2024-H1 model cohorts. The primary estimate is 28.2% (decoder-only models, RMSEA=0.067); the full-population estimate of 31.3–38.1% is an upper bound with poorer IRT fit. This instability persists within every subject domain (within-subject C%=31-45%, avg 38.1%), is not a statistical artifact (random split sanity check: 0.18%), and correlates with domain-specific accuracy improvement (ρ=0.307, p=0.02). ETS threshold sensitivity: C% at {1.0, 2.0, 2.5} thresholds TBD — qualitative finding (>15% substantial instability) must survive across thresholds.
- Evidence: plan_001 (C%=31.3%, enrichment=0.96, sanity=0.18%), plan_010 (arch-stratified C%=28.2%), plan_014 (within-subject C%=38.1%), plan_018 (ETS threshold sensitivity TBD)
- Honesty requirement: ρ=0.307 means "item instability" may mainly reflect "models got better at those domains" — instability decomposition (partial out domain accuracy improvement) TBD
- IRT fit: Lead with decoder-only (RMSEA=0.067, CFI=0.83) as primary; full-population (RMSEA=0.089, CFI=0.78) as upper bound

**Claim 2 (Ground Truth Meta-critique)**: Existing contamination detection literature validates against web-overlap/n-gram labels that measure global exposure (whether an item is publicly accessible), not differential contamination (whether an item functions differently across model cohorts). DIF enrichment≈1.0 against Li et al. labels is expected, not failure — these labels cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. This is a fundamental validation methodology gap: all work using web-overlap labels as ground truth for item-level detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind spot. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF can detect differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5, dose-response from p=0.3 to p=1.0).
- Evidence: plan_001 (enrichment=0.96), plan_011 (ΔTPR=+0.508, dose-response)
- Framing: aggressive — "the field's standard validation approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection"

**Claim 3 (Semi-synthetic Validation Framework)**: The ΔTPR methodology — injecting known differential contamination into real response matrices and measuring detection power increase — provides a controlled validation infrastructure for any item-level contamination detector. Cross-subject matching (using total score on OTHER subjects as MH matching variable) eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 across all 5 tested subjects), while within-subject matching suffers from matching variable contamination (FPR inflation +0.186).

## Strengths (Consensus)

1. **Scale and ambition.** The largest psychometric analysis of an LLM benchmark to date (5,227 models × 12,508 items). The transfer of DIF methodology to this domain is non-trivial and the execution is systematic.

2. **Ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2).** The observation that web-overlap contamination labels measure global exposure, not differential functioning, is the paper's strongest conceptual contribution. ### Critical Issues

1. **ETS threshold uncalibrated for LLM populations (both reviewers).** The |Δ_MH| ≥ 1.5 threshold for ETS C classification is borrowed directly from human educational testing without calibration or sensitivity analysis. The 38% headline number is anchored to this arbitrary cutoff. Without it, a reviewer can reasonably ask: if "instability" is mostly "progress," is this a comparability concern or just evidence that benchmarks are working?

3. **Missing related work (R2, endorsed by R1).** The paper omits several directly relevant lines of work:
   - Measurement invariance literature (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg & Lance 2000) — DIF is a special case of scalar invariance testing
   - MIMIC models (Muthén 1985, Woods 2009) — handles continuous covariates, directly addresses θ-conditioning failure
   - Propensity score matching for DIF (Teresi et al. 2007) — addresses impact-vs-DIF confounding
   - IRT-based DIF methods (Lord's χ², Raju's area) — no justification for MH over these alternatives
   - PSN-IRT (Polo et al., AAAI 2026) — concurrent work applying IRT to MMLU
   - Wang et al. (2026) on RL contamination fragility — directly relevant to RL robustness discussion
   - Tao et al. (2026) on detecting contamination from RL post-training
   
   For a paper claiming to bridge psychometrics and ML evaluation, the psychometric literature coverage is surprisingly thin.

The novelty is empirical (findings) and methodological (framework design), not algorithmic. R1 argues application novelty is legitimate; R2 considers it borderline for a top venue main track. Consensus: the novelty is real but modest, and the paper should be more explicit that its contribution is empirical characterization, not methodological innovation.

The ETS classification's dual requirement (effect size + significance) likely controls this, but the argument is never made explicit. This needs at minimum a paragraph of discussion.

6. **Only uniform DIF detected (R1, endorsed by R2).** MH detects only constant difficulty shifts across ability levels. Non-uniform DIF — where contamination varies by model ability — is plausible (stronger models more likely to have seen specific items) and would be missed entirely. No comparison with logistic regression DIF or SIBTEST is provided.

7. **RL robustness severely underpowered (both reviewers).** N = 13 reasoning-RL models is insufficient to support the "RL robustness" claim. The comparison with per-model detectors (Min-K%, ConStat) is apples-to-oranges: DIF operates at group level and is inherently less sensitive to individual model additions. The paper appropriately places this in the appendix but overclaims in §6 Discussion.

8. **Semi-synthetic injection oversimplified (both reviewers).** Flipping incorrect to correct responses at rate p assumes contamination manifests as deterministic answer knowledge. Real contamination may involve partial knowledge, distractor elimination, or format memorization. The ΔTPR numbers may overestimate detection power against realistic contamination patterns.

# Paper Framing — irt_equated_bench_regen

## Target Venue
- Primary: ICLR 2027 (expected deadline ~October 2026)

## Paper Type
Empirical analysis / psychometric characterization. Discovery paper, not methods paper. "DIF reveals benchmark structural problems," not "DIF detects contamination."

## Core Claims (4 条, 可证伪)

**Claim 1 (Temporal Comparability Concern)**: 28–38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations — they exhibit large DIF (ETS C, |Δ_MH|≥1.5) between 2023 and 2024-H1 model cohorts. The primary estimate is 28.2% (decoder-only models, RMSEA=0.067); the full-population estimate of 31.3–38.1% is an upper bound with poorer IRT fit. This instability persists within every subject domain (within-subject C%=31-45%, avg 38.1%), is not a statistical artifact (random split sanity check: 0.18%), and correlates with domain-specific accuracy improvement (ρ=0.307, p=0.02). ETS threshold sensitivity: C% at {1.0, 2.0, 2.5} thresholds TBD — qualitative finding (>15% substantial instability) must survive across thresholds.
- Evidence: plan_001 (C%=31.3%, enrichment=0.96, sanity=0.18%), plan_010 (arch-stratified C%=28.2%), plan_014 (within-subject C%=38.1%), plan_018 (ETS threshold sensitivity TBD)
- Honesty requirement: ρ=0.307 means "item instability" may mainly reflect "models got better at those domains" — instability decomposition (partial out domain accuracy improvement) TBD
- IRT fit: Lead with decoder-only (RMSEA=0.067, CFI=0.83) as primary; full-population (RMSEA=0.089, CFI=0.78) as upper bound

**Claim 2 (Ground Truth Meta-critique)**: Existing contamination detection literature validates against web-overlap/n-gram labels that measure global exposure (whether an item is publicly accessible), not differential contamination (whether an item functions differently across model cohorts). DIF enrichment≈1.0 against Li et al. labels is expected, not failure — these labels cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. This is a fundamental validation methodology gap: all work using web-overlap labels as ground truth for item-level detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind spot. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF can detect differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5, dose-response from p=0.3 to p=1.0).
- Evidence: plan_001 (enrichment=0.96), plan_011 (ΔTPR=+0.508, dose-response)
- Framing: aggressive — "the field's standard validation approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection"

**Claim 3 (Semi-synthetic Validation Framework)**: The ΔTPR methodology — injecting known differential contamination into real response matrices and measuring detection power increase — provides a controlled validation infrastructure for any item-level contamination detector. Cross-subject matching (using total score on OTHER subjects as MH matching variable) eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 across all 5 tested subjects), while within-subject matching suffers from matching variable contamination (FPR inflation +0.186).
- Evidence: plan_011, plan_016 (ΔFPR=0.000 cross-subject, 4/5 subjects ΔTPR>0.3), plan_004 Step 2 (GSM8K ΔTPR=+0.818 standard, +0.517 external)
- Cross-benchmark: GSM8K replication confirms framework portability to single-domain math benchmarks
- Positioning: cross-subject matching is a practical methodological recommendation; cross-benchmark replication strengthens generalizability

**Claim 4 (Downstream Impact — Four-Layer Finding)**: DIF as diagnostic lens, not quality filter. Four sub-findings:
1. **Benchmark redundancy**: ρ≈0.997 between full and stable-only rankings — MMLU rankings are extremely robust to 31% item removal, revealing massive measurement redundancy in the benchmark.
2. **DIF items = discriminative signal carriers**: DIF removal causes significantly MORE ranking disruption than random removal (z=-8 to -49σ, 21/21 conditions). DIF items carry 1.09× cross-cohort accuracy swing vs 0.96× for stable items — they concentrate the information that differentiates model generations.
3. **DIF as diagnostic lens**: DIF identifies which items' functioning changes most across model generations → reveals which capability dimensions drive ranking shifts. Not "find bad items and remove" but "understand what changed and why." Model-specific patterns: phi-3/llama-3 gain +700-850 ranks from DIF items, mistral merges lose -400 to -587.
4. **Cross-benchmark validation — DIF items resist contamination-based gains**: On GSM8K (1,319 items × 6,702 models), DIF flags anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gap (r=−0.478, p=0.005, 95% CI [−0.71, −0.16]; partial r=−0.394 controlling METABENCH accuracy, p=0.023; permutation p=0.014). Models with larger contamination gaps show disproportionately lower performance on DIF-C items. This is consistent with contamination producing surface-level gains concentrated on non-DIF items, while DIF items capture genuine capability differences.
- Evidence: plan_017 (z=-8 to -49σ, ρ=0.996-0.999), plan_004 Step 3 (r=−0.478, p=0.005, N=33)
- Architecture: plan_017 is load-bearing (strong, full N=5,227), Step 3 adds contamination dimension but is suggestive (N=33, CI wide). If Step 3 attacked, plan_017 stands independently.
- Growing Pains互补: "Growing Pains uses anchor items for efficient evaluation; our DIF diagnostic tells them which anchor items are degrading"
- Caveats (→ limitations): N=33 CI upper bound |r|=0.16 (small effect possible); item difficulty confound not fully excluded (DIF-C items harder for all models); contamination gap is proxy, not ground truth; replication with larger matched sample needed

## Story Spine

**Problem**: LLM benchmarks implicitly assume temporal score comparability — when we say "Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU," we presume both scores reflect the same latent construct. But do they? Item-level behavioral drift across model generations could silently erode this assumption.

**Approach**: We apply Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis — a classical psychometric tool for detecting item-level behavioral anomalies — to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items), the largest-scale DIF analysis on LLM benchmarks to date.

**What we find**: Three discoveries, each a contribution:

1. **38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable** across model generations (ETS C DIF, temporal cohorts). This persists within every subject domain (31-45% per subject), is not statistical noise (random split: 0.18%), and cannot be eliminated by three structural corrections (matched-ability, IRT θ-conditioning, bifactor pre-check). The instability correlates with capability improvement (ρ=0.307) — models got better at those domains, changing how items function.

2. **The field's standard validation approach has a blind spot**: Web-overlap contamination labels (Li et al.) measure whether an item is publicly accessible — a global, model-agnostic property. DIF detects whether an item functions differently across model cohorts — a dynamic, group-specific signal. Enrichment≈1.0 between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is expected when most items have equal global exposure (MMLU on Common Crawl since 2020). Semi-synthetic injection proves DIF works (ΔTPR=+0.508) — the problem is the ground truth, not the detector. Any contamination detection paper validating against web-overlap labels at the item level has the same issue.

3. **A semi-synthetic validation framework** that injects controlled differential contamination into real response matrices, measuring ΔTPR as the detection power metric. Cross-subject matching eliminates the matching variable contamination problem (ΔFPR=0.000). This infrastructure is reusable for validating any item-level contamination detector.

4. **DIF is a diagnostic lens, not a quality filter**. MMLU rankings are massively redundant (ρ≈0.997 after 31% removal), but DIF items concentrate the discriminative signal that differentiates model generations (removal disrupts rankings MORE than random, z=-8 to -49σ). Cross-benchmark validation on GSM8K shows DIF items resist contamination-based performance gains (r=−0.478, 95% CI [−0.71, −0.16]). DIF identifies which capability dimensions are changing — complementing Growing Pains' anchor-item approach by detecting which anchors are degrading.

**Headline result**: "Psychometric analysis of METABENCH reveals that 38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations. Web-overlap contamination labels do not capture this differential signal (enrichment≈1.0), while semi-synthetic injection confirms detection capability (ΔTPR=+0.508 on MMLU, +0.818 on GSM8K). Cross-benchmark validation using GSM1K contamination gaps shows DIF items resist contamination-based performance gains (r=−0.478, 95% CI [−0.71, −0.16]; partial r=−0.394 controlling accuracy). We provide a reusable validation framework with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000)."

## Empirical Observation: Structural Constraints on DIF in LLM Benchmarks

Systematic experimentation reveals that three structural improvements — matched-ability cohort design (plan_001b), IRT θ-conditioning (plan_012, r=0.9986), and bifactor pre-check (plan_014, within-subject C%=38.1%) — all fail to reduce temporal DIF baseline FPR below 31% while maintaining detection power. This is an empirical observation, not a formal impossibility result. The constraints arise from: (a) unidimensional IRT limitations in modeling 57-subject multidimensional ability, (b) statistical power requirements (N≥80, δ≥1.4), and (c) inability to separate ability confounding from genuine item-level changes. Higher-level methods (MIMIC, propensity-score matching, multidimensional IRT) may address individual constraints — future work.

## Venue Fit

- **ICLR 2027**: Good fit — empirical analysis of evaluation methodology, psychometric rigor, large-scale characterization. Risk: ML reviewers may not be familiar with DIF/IRT. Mitigation: §3 provides self-contained DIF primer with ML translations.
- **Novelty concern**: DIF itself is not new (1988). Our contributions are: (1) the empirical finding of 28–38% instability at unprecedented scale (5,227×12,508), (2) the ground truth meta-critique affecting the field's validation methodology, (3) the semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject matching innovation (ΔFPR=0.000), (4) DIF as diagnostic lens revealing benchmark measurement structure. Explicitly acknowledge MH-DIF is applied without modification; novelty is empirical characterization + framework design, not algorithmic. Frame as "bringing mature psychometric tools to characterize an urgent ML evaluation problem — the scale creates novel statistical challenges (architecture heterogeneity, multidimensional construct, 5000+ examinees)."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns (updated for pivot)

1. **"38% could just mean models got better"** — Yes, partially. ρ=0.307 confirms correlation. We discuss this honestly. The contribution is the finding itself: benchmarks have massive item-level behavioral drift, regardless of cause.

2. **"Ground truth critique is obvious — of course web labels don't capture differential effects"** — Not obvious: the field routinely uses these labels for item-level validation. We provide the first empirical demonstration with both the enrichment≈1.0 result and the semi-synthetic proof of concept.

3. **"Semi-synthetic injection is artificial"** — We inject into real response matrices (not simulated), preserving real ability distributions and item characteristics. The mechanism (incorrect→correct flipping) is a simplification acknowledged in limitations.

4. **"DIF power is only sufficient for large effects"** — Large effects are precisely what threaten benchmark validity most. Operational region: N≥80, δ≥1.4, TPR=0.68-0.80.

5. **"Only validated on MMLU"** — Partially addressed: GSM8K replication (METABENCH 1,319 items × 6,702 models) confirms semi-synthetic framework portability (ΔTPR=+0.818) and temporal DIF pattern (C%=18.9%). GSM1K contamination gap validation (N=33) provides cross-benchmark evidence. Full generalization to diverse benchmarks remains future work.

6. **"Higher methods (MIMIC, propensity-score) could solve the confounding"** — Acknowledged as future work. We frame our three-attempt negative results as "empirical observation" that motivates these directions, not as impossibility.

7. **"ETS threshold is uncalibrated for LLM populations"** — Report C% at {1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5} thresholds. Show qualitative finding (>15% instability) is robust across cutoffs. This is the #1 missing analysis per Dream #3.

8. **"Multiple testing: 12,508 simultaneous tests without correction"** — ETS classification provides implicit protection via dual requirement (effect size ≥1.5 + significance). Random-split sanity check (C%=0.18%, ~22 items on 12,508) empirically demonstrates FPR control. Report BH-corrected C% as robustness check.

9. **"Only uniform DIF — non-uniform DIF plausible for LLMs"** — Apply SIBTEST or logistic regression DIF to 5-10 representative subjects as robustness check. Show MH results are not missing substantial non-uniform DIF.

10. **"Ranking disruption result is tautological"** — Circularity ablation: compare DIF removal disruption vs (a) highest raw accuracy gap, (b) highest item discrimination, (c) highest variance items. If DIF uniquely disrupts beyond these baselines, circularity concern is addressed.

## Dropped from Original Framing

- **Ensemble (Claim 2 old)**: plan_003a/b/c never executed. Future work.
- **Regeneration (Claim 3 old)**: Bifactor killed by plan_014 pre-check. Dropped entirely.
- **RL robustness**: Theoretically motivated but N=13 insufficient. Limitations disclosure, not claim.
- **Detection as primary contribution**: Pivoted from "we detect contamination" to "we characterize benchmark properties."

# Dream Review Report: Psychometric Characterization of Item Instability in LLM Benchmarks

**Paper**: Psychometric Characterization of Item Instability in LLM Benchmarks: A Large-Scale Differential Item Functioning Analysis of MMLU  
**Review mode**: Full (2-reviewer roundtable)  
**Date**: 2026-05-21  
**Venue standard**: Top ML venue, ~25% acceptance, 6-point scale

---

## Roundtable Summary

Two reviewers independently scored the paper **4/6** (Weak Accept). After cross-sharing and discussion, R1 revised down to **3/6** (Weak Reject) citing novelty gaps and the undermined central narrative (ρ=0.307 suggests instability is partly capability improvement). R2 held at **4/6** but acknowledged the paper needs major revision. The consensus is **Borderline Reject (3–4/6)** — the paper addresses an important problem with commendable experimental rigor and intellectual honesty, but methodological gaps, limited novelty, and an underdeveloped central narrative prevent acceptance in current form.

---

## Final Scores

| Dimension | R1 | R2 | Consensus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soundness | 3/4 | — | 3/4 |
| Empirical Rigor | 3/4 | — | 3/4 |
| Novelty | — | 2/4 | 2/4 |
| Significance | — | 3/4 | 3/4 |
| Clarity | — | 3/4 | 3/4 |
| **Overall** | **3/6** | **4/6** | **3.5/6 (Borderline Reject)** |
| Confidence | 4/5 | 4/5 | 4/5 |

---

## Strengths (Consensus)

1. **Scale and ambition.** The largest psychometric analysis of an LLM benchmark to date (5,227 models × 12,508 items). The transfer of DIF methodology to this domain is non-trivial and the execution is systematic.

2. **Ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2).** The observation that web-overlap contamination labels measure global exposure, not differential functioning, is the paper's strongest conceptual contribution. It affects the validation methodology of Min-K%, ConStat, DVD, and all work using web-overlap as item-level ground truth. Both reviewers consider this independently valuable.

3. **Semi-synthetic validation framework (Claim 3).** The cross-subject matching innovation (ΔFPR = 0.000) is a clean, practical methodological contribution. The insight that matching on within-subject total score contaminates the matching variable is subtle and empirically well-demonstrated.

4. **Thorough controls and honest reporting.** Random-split sanity checks (C% = 0.18% vs. temporal 31.3%), architecture-stratified analysis (C% drops to 22.1% with improved IRT fit), dose-response curves, permutation tests, and leave-one-out robustness analyses. The transparent treatment of negative results (three structural corrections failed) is above average for the venue.

5. **DIF as diagnostic lens (Claim 4).** Supported by two independent evidence lines: (a) DIF item removal disrupts rankings more than random removal (z = −8 to −49σ), and (b) DIF flags anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gaps (r = −0.478, p = 0.005). This reframing from "find bad items" to "understand what changed" is well-argued.

6. **Architecture stratification (§4.3).** Transforms a potential fatal objection into a practical recommendation. The 29% C% reduction with dramatically improved IRT fit (RMSEA 0.082 → 0.037) is the paper's most methodologically satisfying experiment.

---

## Weaknesses (Consensus)

### Critical Issues

1. **ETS threshold uncalibrated for LLM populations (both reviewers).** The |Δ_MH| ≥ 1.5 threshold for ETS C classification is borrowed directly from human educational testing without calibration or sensitivity analysis. The 38% headline number is anchored to this arbitrary cutoff. If the threshold were 2.0, the finding would change substantially. **The paper must report C% at multiple thresholds (e.g., 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5) to demonstrate qualitative robustness.** This is the single most important missing analysis.

2. **ρ = 0.307 undermines the central narrative (both reviewers).** The correlation between C% and subject-level accuracy improvement suggests a substantial fraction of "instability" is models genuinely getting better at specific domains. The paper frames this honestly but does not adequately decompose capability-improvement DIF from genuine measurement anomaly DIF. A partial correlation or regression decomposition is needed. Without it, a reviewer can reasonably ask: if "instability" is mostly "progress," is this a comparability concern or just evidence that benchmarks are working?

3. **Missing related work (R2, endorsed by R1).** The paper omits several directly relevant lines of work:
   - Measurement invariance literature (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg & Lance 2000) — DIF is a special case of scalar invariance testing
   - MIMIC models (Muthén 1985, Woods 2009) — handles continuous covariates, directly addresses θ-conditioning failure
   - Propensity score matching for DIF (Teresi et al. 2007) — addresses impact-vs-DIF confounding
   - IRT-based DIF methods (Lord's χ², Raju's area) — no justification for MH over these alternatives
   - PSN-IRT (Polo et al., AAAI 2026) — concurrent work applying IRT to MMLU
   - Wang et al. (2026) on RL contamination fragility — directly relevant to RL robustness discussion
   - Tao et al. (2026) on detecting contamination from RL post-training
   
   For a paper claiming to bridge psychometrics and ML evaluation, the psychometric literature coverage is surprisingly thin.

4. **No algorithmic novelty (R2, partially contested by R1).** The core method is off-the-shelf MH-DIF applied to a binary response matrix — a direct application of a 40-year-old technique. The novelty is empirical (findings) and methodological (framework design), not algorithmic. R1 argues application novelty is legitimate; R2 considers it borderline for a top venue main track. Consensus: the novelty is real but modest, and the paper should be more explicit that its contribution is empirical characterization, not methodological innovation.

### Major Issues

5. **Multiple testing not addressed (R1, endorsed by R2).** 12,508 simultaneous MH tests with no Bonferroni, FDR, or other correction. The ETS classification's dual requirement (effect size + significance) likely controls this, but the argument is never made explicit. This needs at minimum a paragraph of discussion.

6. **Only uniform DIF detected (R1, endorsed by R2).** MH detects only constant difficulty shifts across ability levels. Non-uniform DIF — where contamination varies by model ability — is plausible (stronger models more likely to have seen specific items) and would be missed entirely. No comparison with logistic regression DIF or SIBTEST is provided.

7. **RL robustness severely underpowered (both reviewers).** N = 13 reasoning-RL models is insufficient to support the "RL robustness" claim. The comparison with per-model detectors (Min-K%, ConStat) is apples-to-oranges: DIF operates at group level and is inherently less sensitive to individual model additions. The paper appropriately places this in the appendix but overclaims in §6 Discussion.

8. **Semi-synthetic injection oversimplified (both reviewers).** Flipping incorrect to correct responses at rate p assumes contamination manifests as deterministic answer knowledge. Real contamination may involve partial knowledge, distractor elimination, or format memorization. The ΔTPR numbers may overestimate detection power against realistic contamination patterns.

9. **Cumulative Bayesian DIF speculative (both reviewers).** §5.3 introduces a Bayesian DIF accumulation framework that is entirely simulated with no validation on actual METABENCH temporal data. Insufficient methodological detail (prior specification, batch ordering sensitivity, threshold sensitivity). Feels like a separate, underdeveloped contribution stapled onto the paper.

### Minor Issues

10. **GSM1K validation sample size.** N = 33 matched models with wide confidence interval (~[−0.70, −0.17] at 95%). The anti-correlation finding is directionally convincing but imprecise.

11. **Bifactor TLI = 0.89** is below the conventional 0.90 acceptability threshold, yet equating results from this model are presented without adequate caveat.

12. **Paper scope too broad.** Four claims + architecture stratification + structural constraints + Bayesian DIF + RL robustness + cross-benchmark validation + future work with pilot results (Tables 7–11). Each receives insufficient depth. The Future Work section is disproportionately long with preliminary numbers that feel like padding.

13. **Growing Pains comparison not empirically tested.** The paper claims DIF "complements" Growing Pains' anchor-item approach but does not test C% among Growing Pains' specific anchor items.

---

## Questions for Authors

1. What is C% at alternative ETS thresholds (|Δ_MH| ≥ 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5)? Does the qualitative finding (>20% instability) survive across thresholds?

2. If you partial out accuracy improvement from C%, what fraction of the 38% instability remains unexplained by capability gains?

3. Why MH-DIF specifically rather than logistic regression DIF, which naturally accommodates continuous covariates and would have avoided the θ-conditioning failure?

4. For cross-subject matching ΔFPR = 0.000: is this exactly zero or rounded? Across how many injection levels and seeds?

5. What drives the 9.2pp C% reduction in architecture stratification — removal of non-decoder models, or the smaller sample size (3,847 vs. 5,227)?

6. What is the C% among Growing Pains' specific anchor items?

7. For Cumulative Bayesian DIF: how sensitive is TPR/FPR to the Bayes factor threshold (2.0 vs. 3.2 vs. 5.0)?

8. How does restricting to models above a minimum accuracy threshold affect C%? Very weak models (near-random) may inflate DIF statistics.

---

## Experiment Coverage Assessment

**Executed and included in paper:**
- Core temporal DIF analysis — ✅ Main text §4.1
- Architecture-stratified DIF (plan_010) — ✅ Main text §4.3, strong
- Semi-synthetic validation — ✅ Main text §4.4
- Structural constraints / bifactor (plan_005 partial) — ✅ §4.5
- Benchmark redundancy / diagnostic lens (plan_017) — ✅ §5.1
- Cross-benchmark GSM8K validation — ✅ §5.2
- Cumulative Bayesian DIF (plan_007) — ✅ §5.3, underdeveloped
- RL robustness (plan_002) — ✅ Appendix A, underpowered (N=13)
- Item-Focused Trees (plan_009) — ✅ Appendix B

**Dropped but pilot results reported in Future Work:**
- ConStat (plan_003a) — Table 8
- DVD (plan_003b) — Table 9
- Ensemble fusion (plan_003c) — Table 7
- Item generation (plan_006) — Table 11
- Graceful degradation (plan_008) — Table 10

The paper covers the core experiments adequately. The dropped experiments are appropriately positioned as future work. The main coverage gap is not missing experiments but missing **sensitivity analyses** on the experiments that were run (threshold sensitivity, temporal boundary sensitivity, model quality filtering).

---

## Recommendations for Revision

**Must-fix for resubmission:**
1. Add ETS threshold sensitivity analysis (C% at multiple cutoffs)
2. Decompose instability: partial out capability improvement from C%
3. Expand related work with measurement invariance, MIMIC, IRT-based DIF alternatives
4. Add multiple testing discussion
5. Either strengthen RL robustness with more models or downgrade claims to "preliminary observation"

**Strongly recommended:**
6. Include at least one non-uniform DIF method comparison (logistic regression DIF)
7. Tighten scope: move Bayesian DIF and some Future Work tables to supplementary
8. Test C% among Growing Pains anchor items
9. Add one more benchmark beyond MMLU and GSM8K

**If space permits:**
10. Discuss alternative injection mechanisms and their implications for ΔTPR estimates
11. Report model quality filtering sensitivity
12. Report temporal boundary sensitivity

---

## Final Verdict

**Borderline Reject (3.5/6).** The paper tackles an important problem — whether LLM benchmark scores remain comparable across model generations — and brings rigorous psychometric methodology to bear on it at unprecedented scale. The ground truth meta-critique, cross-subject matching innovation, and architecture stratification analysis are genuine contributions. However, the 38% headline finding rests on an uncalibrated threshold with no sensitivity analysis, the central narrative is partially undermined by the capability-improvement correlation (ρ = 0.307), the related work has significant gaps, and the paper overextends by trying to present too many results without sufficient depth on any. With a focused revision addressing threshold sensitivity, instability decomposition, and related work coverage, this could become a solid contribution. In current form, the methodological gaps and limited novelty place it below the acceptance threshold for a top ML venue.

# Paper Framing — irt_equated_bench_regen

## Target Venue
- Primary: ICLR 2027 (expected deadline ~October 2026)

## Paper Type
Empirical analysis / psychometric characterization. Discovery paper, not methods paper. "DIF reveals benchmark structural problems," not "DIF detects contamination."

## Core Claims (4 条, 可证伪)

**Claim 1 (Temporal Comparability Concern)**: 31–38% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations — they exhibit large DIF (ETS C, |Δ_MH|≥1.5) between 2023 and 2024-H1 model cohorts. Primary estimate: 31.3% (temporal cohort, plan_001); within-subject range 31-45%, avg 38.1% (plan_014). This instability is not a statistical artifact (random split sanity check: 0.18%), and correlates with domain-specific accuracy improvement (ρ=0.307, p=0.02). Architecture-stratified estimate (decoder-only subset) TBD — plan_010 not yet executed. ETS threshold sensitivity: C% at {1.0, 2.0, 2.5} thresholds TBD — qualitative finding (>15% substantial instability) must survive across thresholds.
- Evidence: plan_001 (C%=31.3%, enrichment=0.96, sanity=0.18%), plan_014 (within-subject C%=38.1%), plan_010 (arch-stratified TBD), plan_018 (ETS threshold sensitivity TBD)
- Honesty requirement: ρ=0.307 means "item instability" may mainly reflect "models got better at those domains" — instability decomposition (partial out domain accuracy improvement) TBD
- IRT fit: Full-population fit indices TBD from plan_010; if decoder-only fit substantially improves, lead with that subset as primary

**Claim 2 (Ground Truth Meta-critique)**: Existing contamination detection literature validates against web-overlap/n-gram labels that measure global exposure (whether an item is publicly accessible), not differential contamination (whether an item functions differently across model cohorts). DIF enrichment≈1.0 against Li et al. labels is expected, not failure — these labels cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. This is a fundamental validation methodology gap: all work using web-overlap labels as ground truth for item-level detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind spot. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF can detect differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5, dose-response from p=0.3 to p=1.0).
- Evidence: plan_001 (enrichment=0.96), plan_011 (ΔTPR=+0.508, dose-response)
- Framing: aggressive — "the field's standard validation approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection"

**Claim 3 (Semi-synthetic Validation Framework)**: The ΔTPR methodology — injecting known differential contamination into real response matrices and measuring detection power increase — provides a controlled validation infrastructure for any item-level contamination detector. Cross-subject matching (using total score on OTHER subjects as MH matching variable) eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 across all 5 tested subjects), while within-subject matching suffers from matching variable contamination (FPR inflation +0.186).

  summary: MVP DIF 检测采用 ETS C 分类（效应量+显著性双阈值）替代 BH 校正 p 值作为主判定标准

    δ≥1.4 与 GSM1K 文档的重度污染效应量吻合。小效应由 ensemble 其他信号覆盖。

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
